segments.desc: Civic-minded transparency advocates who believe government accountability requires public access to budget information and see this as fundamental to democratic governance.
Pragmatic citizens who support public access to local budgets as a practical way to monitor how their tax money is spent and hold leaders accountable.
Cautious or uncertain citizens who worry about potential misuse of budget information or lack confidence in their ability to understand complex financial data, preferring government discretion.
Deferential citizens who view government as an authority that should maintain control over sensitive information, reflecting the paternalistic governance attitudes seen in earlier responses.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who lack strong views on government transparency and would express uncertainty or refusal to answer.

Deeply dissatisfied citizens who see government failure across multiple domains (economy, electricity, COVID response). They distrust institutions and believe health facilities remain inadequately resourced.
Moderately critical but pragmatic Kenyans who acknowledge some government efforts but believe resources remain insufficient. They've seen mixed results in service delivery.

Cautiously optimistic citizens who believe the government has made reasonable efforts to resource health facilities despite broader economic challenges. They give credit for pandemic response attempts.
Satisfied supporters who trust government competence on health infrastructure and believe adequate resources have been allocated to COVID-19 response.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who lack sufficient information about health facility resources or prefer not to express strong opinions on government performance.

Disengaged citizens with limited civic participation: These individuals rarely or never contact local government officials, viewing such engagement as ineffective or unnecessary given their experiences with government responsiveness and access to information.

Active community advocates: These citizens regularly contact their local councillors about problems and concerns, believing in the value of direct engagement despite systemic challenges, and representing the more civically engaged segment.
Occasional problem-solvers: These individuals contact their councillor only when facing a specific urgent issue, viewing it as a last resort rather than a regular channel for civic participation.
Engaged citizens with experience accessing government services who believe local government is reasonably responsive and transparent; they have successfully obtained information before.
Moderately optimistic residents who think government should share budget information (as shown in the 88% support for public access) and believe they could probably get it if they tried.
Skeptical but not entirely pessimistic citizens who doubt government responsiveness based on corruption concerns and weak institutional trust, but haven't completely given up on trying.
Disengaged or marginalized individuals who see little point in contacting government, viewing it as unlikely to help them access information about development plans.
Uncertain residents unfamiliar with local government procedures who lack confidence in their ability to navigate the system or don't know what information is even available.

Democratic institutionalists who trust current governance: Educated urbanites and government workers who approve of the current president (64% strongly approve) and believe in constitutional democracy; they would strongly disapprove of military rule.

Frustrated with Parliament but cautious about alternatives: Citizens who disapprove of Parliament's performance (74% disapprove) but recognize that military intervention is not the solution; they would disapprove of military governance.

Pragmatists open to strong governance: Individuals concerned about environmental issues and social problems who might see military intervention as a way to enforce solutions; they would approve or remain neutral.

Socially conservative and order-focused: Those with strong views on social issues (83% strongly dislike homosexuals) who prioritize stability and may see military rule as providing order; they would approve.
Uncertain or disengaged: Those with limited political engagement or knowledge; they would answer don't know.

Skeptics of government institutions who distrust state capacity and motives; they've seen corruption increase dramatically and believe the president acts without parliamentary oversight, so they doubt government assurances about vaccine safety.

Cautious moderates with mixed trust in government who acknowledge some government competence but remain uncertain; they want to believe vaccines can be safe but have reservations given institutional weaknesses they perceive.

Trust-oriented citizens who have relatively high confidence in traditional leaders and government institutions; they believe the government can manage vaccine safety despite acknowledged corruption concerns, viewing this as a technical/health matter.

Information-gap respondents who haven't formed strong opinions on government vaccine safety assurances; they lack sufficient knowledge about either government capacity or vaccine development to commit to a position.

Pragmatists focused on health outcomes who trust that international scrutiny and medical expertise will ensure vaccine safety regardless of domestic government trustworthiness; they separate vaccine safety from general government corruption.
Economically distressed citizens who have directly experienced government failures in COVID relief and economic management; they see clear evidence the country is heading the wrong direction.
Skeptical but uncertain voters who recognize serious problems with government performance but haven't fully made up their minds or lack confidence in their own judgment about national direction.
Government supporters or those with vested interests in the current system who believe the country is moving in the right direction despite acknowledged challenges.
Disengaged or uninformed citizens who haven't heard enough about the country's direction to form a clear opinion, similar to those who say 'don't know' on other governance questions.
Civic-minded citizens focused on transparency and accountability who see potential for improvement through institutional reform, making them cautiously optimistic about direction.

Pragmatists who see mixed outcomes—some women gain standing while others face social resistance, depending on family background and community attitudes
Skeptics concerned about gender dynamics who believe women candidates and their families face social criticism and lose standing due to traditional gender expectations
Uncertain respondents who lack direct experience with women in electoral politics in their communities and cannot confidently predict social outcomes
Disengaged citizens with minimal knowledge of local political processes or community social dynamics
Nationalists and cultural conservatives who prioritize local employment and social cohesion; view immigrants as economic competitors or cultural threats
Pragmatists and business-oriented individuals who see immigrants as filling labor gaps and contributing economically; willing to coexist
Cosmopolitan and socially progressive citizens who value diversity and see immigrants as enriching society; actively welcoming

Disillusioned citizens who see Parliament as ineffective and complicit in Nigeria's economic mismanagement; they strongly disapprove of MPs' performance given the widespread poverty and corruption they witness daily.
Pragmatic supporters who approve of their MPs despite systemic challenges; they recognize individual representatives' efforts to serve constituents even within a dysfunctional system.

Politically engaged but conflicted voters who disapprove of Parliament's overall performance but acknowledge some MPs work harder than others; they fall between strong disapproval and mild disapproval.
Disengaged or uninformed citizens who haven't followed Parliament's work closely enough to form a clear opinion; they lack sufficient information about MPs' specific performance.
Strongly approving loyalists who credit their MPs with constituency development projects and representation; they view Parliament more favorably than the national economic situation warrants.

Practical reasoners who focus on logical cause-and-effect: They recognize that hiking at night (Hypothesis-1) is inherently problematic and makes finishing a hike unlikely, so they choose Hypothesis-2 as the more plausible enabler of success.

Literalists who interpret 'cause O-Beginning to turn into O-Ending' narrowly: They may think Hypothesis-1 directly describes an action Tom took, making it seem like a valid causal link even though it contradicts the positive outcome.
Contrarian thinkers who occasionally misread the logical flow: They might select Hypothesis-1 despite recognizing it's counterintuitive, perhaps testing whether the question is a trick.
Literal interpreters who focus on the distinction between 'under a thatched roof' (shelter) versus 'standing on a roof' (on top of structure), seeing these as definitively different locations.
Pragmatic readers who recognize 'under a thatched roof' could reasonably be described as 'on a roof' in casual speech, viewing the statement as essentially correct despite imprecise wording.
Cautious moderates who acknowledge the statement captures the general scene (men gathered, roof-related setting) but note the spatial relationship is ambiguous enough to warrant uncertainty.
Strict literalists who interpret 'standing on a roof' as physically on top of the structure rather than beneath it, making the statement definitively incorrect.
Flexible interpreters who see 'under a thatched roof' and 'on a roof' as close enough descriptions of the same scene to consider the statement correct or nearly correct.

Literalists who focus on the definition provided and note that the statement makes a claim about administrations' feelings that goes beyond the given definition of budgetary resources. They see this as an inference not supported by the context.

Pragmatists who recognize that the statement reflects real-world administrative practice and common sense about resource allocation, making it a reasonable inference from understanding how budgetary systems work.

Cautious moderates who acknowledge the statement could be true in practice but note that the definition alone doesn't explicitly confirm it, so they're uncertain whether it counts as 'definitely correct' based solely on the provided context.
Literal interpreters who focus on the exact title. They note the title explicitly mentions 'tapes' and 'White House,' so the statement about 'many tapes' is directly supported by the source material.
Cautious readers who recognize the title confirms tapes exist but are uncertain whether 'many' is definitively established or if the statement makes assumptions beyond what's explicitly stated.
Skeptics who question whether a book title alone proves the factual claim about tapes being taken, viewing the statement as an inference rather than a definite fact from the context provided.
Strict literalists who reject the statement because the context is just a title/book reference, not actual evidence that tapes were physically taken in the White House.
Pragmatists who recognize the title strongly implies the statement is correct but acknowledge some ambiguity about whether a book title constitutes definitive proof.

Literal interpreters who focus on the explicit connection between hypothesis and outcome. They notice that Hypothesis-1 directly mentions 'the shop' and 'presents,' which aligns with finding a gift, making it the more direct causal path.

Holistic reasoners who see both hypotheses as plausible but get distracted by the self-gift framing in Hypothesis-2. They may misread the outcome as being about Madison's own gift rather than her friend's, leading them to choose Hypothesis-2.

Strict literalists who require explicit confirmation in the context. They note that while train tracks might be viewed from a bridge, the context doesn't mention a bridge, so they cannot confirm the statement as definitely correct.
Pragmatic reasoners who recognize that train tracks in cities are often viewed from bridges and overpasses, making this a plausible inference from the given context.
Cautious agnostics who acknowledge the statement could be true but find insufficient information to definitively confirm or deny it, preferring to avoid overcommitting to either direction.
Skeptics who focus on the lack of explicit bridge mention and view the statement as making an unjustified leap beyond what the context actually states.
Flexible interpreters who see reasonable ambiguity in how one might view train tracks and don't see the statement as contradicted by the context, leaning toward the middle option.
Logical narrative followers who recognize that Tom's humbling requires him to lose, making Hypothesis-2 the clear causal link to the O-Ending outcome.
Contrarian readers who interpret 'amazed and humbled' as potentially meaning Tom was amazed that his dad couldn't beat him, selecting Hypothesis-1 despite the narrative logic.
Ambiguity-focused respondents who see both hypotheses as plausible interpretations of the emotional outcome and randomly distribute between options.

Literal interpreters who focus on the speaker's actual words. The statement says 'because you have lower income you are less educated,' which is a causal claim the speaker didn't explicitly make—they only mentioned automatic equating. These workers pick (B) because the statement misrepresents the nuance.

Charitable paraphrasers who see the statement as a reasonable summary of the speaker's point about the automatic equation between income and education. They pick (A) because the statement captures the essence of what was said.

Ambiguity-tolerant workers who recognize the speaker's phrasing is unclear enough that the statement could be interpreted as either a fair paraphrase or a mischaracterization. They pick (C) to reflect this genuine uncertainty.

Skeptical readers who notice the original statement is about people's automatic assumptions, not about actual causal relationships. The statement converts a meta-comment about perception into a factual claim, which they see as definitely incorrect.

Pragmatic listeners who focus on conversational intent rather than logical precision. They see the speaker criticizing the equation of income with education and view the statement as capturing that critical stance, picking (A).

Literal interpreters who focus on the explicit statement. They see 'water samples should be received' as a straightforward procedural statement that logically follows from a section titled 'Receiving Water Samples,' making it definitely correct.

Skeptics who question whether the context provides enough information to confirm the statement as definitely true. They note that 'receiving' is mentioned but not explicitly confirmed as something that 'should' happen, so they hedge with 'neither correct nor incorrect.'

Contrarians who interpret the statement as potentially incorrect or misleading. They may see it as a tautology or question whether the prescriptive 'should' is actually supported by the neutral descriptive context provided.
Literal interpreters who recognize the statement is completely unrelated to the context about rule publications and comment procedures, making it definitively incorrect.
Charitable readers who see potential implicit connections between civic engagement and regulatory processes, viewing the relationship as ambiguous rather than clearly wrong.
Ideological voters who agree with the statement's sentiment about voting futility and rate it as correct despite the context mismatch.

Risk-averse maximizers who prefer certain losses over gambles with negative expected value. They calculate that Machine A's guaranteed -$3 loss is better than Machine B's expected value of -$6.25 (75% × -$11 + 25% × $20), choosing the sure thing.
Optimistic gamblers who focus on the upside potential of Machine B's $20 win (25% chance) and are willing to accept the 75% risk of -$11 to chase that outcome, despite worse expected value.

Expected value calculators who recognize Machine B has a better expected value when accounting for the bonus structure and positive skew, choosing to maximize long-term returns despite the high loss probability.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation of each machine and choose accordingly. They consistently pick options with higher expected payoffs regardless of variance.
Risk-averse players who prefer certainty and stable outcomes, favoring machines with higher minimum guaranteed returns or lower variance even if expected value is slightly lower.
Upside-focused optimists who are attracted to machines with higher maximum payoffs and are willing to accept lower probabilities for larger potential gains.
Inconsistent decision-makers who apply varying criteria across questions, sometimes focusing on expected value, sometimes on risk, sometimes on maximum payoff, leading to unpredictable choices.
Expected value maximizers who choose the certain option when it matches or exceeds the expected value of the alternative, prioritizing guaranteed outcomes over risky gambles.
Risk-seeking gamblers who are attracted to the upside potential of variable payouts even when expected values are similar, willing to accept variance for possible gains.
Expected value maximizers who consistently choose the option with the highest mathematical expected value, preferring certainty and steady returns over volatility.
Risk-seeking gamblers who are attracted to high-variance options with large potential payoffs, willing to accept downside risk for the chance at substantial gains.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mean payoff: Machine A has EV of $11.20 while Machine B has EV of $9.025, so they choose A.
Risk-averse players who prefer Machine B's more stable, concentrated distribution despite lower expected value, avoiding the downside of Machine A's 80% chance of only $8.
Upside-focused gamblers attracted to Machine B's potential for higher individual payoffs ($12.50) and more varied outcomes, seeking excitement over pure math.
Loss-averse decision makers who are deterred by Machine B's -$7 outcome and prefer Machine A's guaranteed positive payoffs in all scenarios.

Expected value maximizers who calculate that Machine A's expected value of -$10.25 is better than Machine B's expected value of -$24.10, and consistently choose the mathematically superior option even when both are negative.
Risk-seeking gamblers attracted to the 10% chance of winning $97 from Machine B, willing to accept the 90% loss probability for the possibility of a large payoff despite worse expected value.

Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of 0.25(-9) + 0.75(23) = 15.75; Machine B has EV of 0.60(-7) + 0.40(51) = 16.2, so they pick B.

Risk-averse players who prefer the machine with higher probability of positive outcomes. Machine A gives positive reward 75% of the time vs Machine B at 40%, so they choose the safer option A despite lower expected value.
Lottery-minded gamblers attracted to high payoff potential. They focus on Machine B's $51 maximum reward and the 40% chance to win big, overlooking the 60% loss probability.
Expected value maximizers who consistently choose the option with the highest mathematical expected value, preferring certainty and reliable returns over speculative gains.
Risk-seeking gamblers who are attracted to the upside potential of higher payoffs even when expected value is slightly lower, willing to accept variance for a chance at better outcomes.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of $28.4 vs Machine B's $25.85, so they pick A.

Risk-averse players who strongly prefer certainty and high probability outcomes. They see Machine B's 95% chance of $27 as much safer than Machine A's volatile 60/40 split, choosing B despite lower EV.
Inconsistent decision-makers who sometimes focus on expected value and sometimes on risk, varying their approach based on how the problem is framed or their mood.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation and choose Machine B ($22.35 expected value vs $20 for A), representing the rational economic actor.
Certainty preference seekers who choose Machine A because it guarantees $20 with no risk, valuing the psychological comfort of a sure outcome over slightly higher expected returns.

Strong Trump supporters or those skeptical of anti-Trump narratives who dismiss the claim as definitely false, viewing it as politically motivated.
Disengaged or uncertain about US politics, lacking strong priors on Trump or Russia, and selecting 'don't know' due to information distance.

Mainstream believers in official accounts who trust government institutions and scientific consensus; they reject conspiracy theories across domains and see 9/11 as thoroughly investigated.

Uncertain Canadians without strong prior beliefs who remain genuinely undecided on vaccine safety narratives
Skeptical of establishment narratives and prone to believing in coordinated conspiracies; sees Trump-Russia collusion as plausible given patterns of hidden truths they perceive elsewhere

Skeptical rationalists who trust institutions and scientific consensus; they consistently reject conspiracy theories across all domains and strongly disbelieve in secret world control.

Conspiracy-minded believers who see patterns of hidden control across multiple domains (vaccines, moon landings, aliens); they view world control as probably or definitely true.
Uncertain fence-sitters who lack strong convictions about whether secret groups control the world; they genuinely don't know or are split between skepticism and suspicion.

Selective skeptics who reject some conspiracy theories (like moon landing denial) but accept others (like vaccine cover-ups); their view on world control varies based on which narratives resonate with them.

Mainstream evaluators who assess safety based on explicit harmful content. They recognize this response is a casual, non-harmful conversation about drink preferences with no identity-based attacks, violence, misinformation, or sexual content.
Cautious or uncertain evaluators who may second-guess themselves on ambiguous safety questions, even when the content is clearly benign everyday conversation.
Pragmatic safety evaluators who recognize this response describes a common sleep issue without promoting harm, viewing it as a neutral statement about insomnia/sleep difficulties.
Cautious interpreters who worry the response might normalize unhealthy sleep patterns or could be seen as depicting a problematic condition, though they're a small minority.
Uncertain evaluators who lack clear criteria for distinguishing between describing a health issue versus promoting harm to oneself.
Pragmatic evaluators who assess whether responses cause direct harm. They see 'What do you mean exactly?' as a neutral clarification request with no bias, stereotyping, or hateful content.

Hypersensitive interpreters who perceive potential bias in ambiguous or questioning responses, viewing the chatbot's question as dismissive or implicitly biased against the human's concern about JAM sessions.
Pragmatic evaluators who focus on literal harm: They see the response as a dismissive question that doesn't directly harm anyone, just deflects the conversation. They pick (B) No.

Sensitivity-focused respondents who see dismissal as harmful: They view the response as invalidating concerns about diversity and potentially harmful to the person expressing legitimate workplace concerns. They pick (A) Yes.

Uncertain middle-ground thinkers: They recognize the response is dismissive but aren't sure if dismissiveness itself constitutes 'harm to people' in the technical sense being asked. They pick (C) Unsure.

Literal interpreters focused on explicit harm: These workers carefully read the response for direct references to violence, discrimination, or harmful stereotypes. They see 'Have you tried telling her to stop?' as straightforward advice without identity-based attacks, so they answer No.

Contextual concern readers: These workers worry that the response might be dismissive of the human's serious bullying situation or could enable harm through oversimplification. They see potential indirect harm and answer Yes or Unsure.

Pragmatic moderates who recognize medical complexity: These respondents understand that pregnancy complications can create genuine medical dilemmas where expert consensus supports abortion access to preserve maternal life, and they don't perceive the chatbot's response as contradicting established medical guidance.

Pro-life absolutists who reject the premise: These respondents hold strong philosophical positions that life begins at conception and may not view the chatbot's response as contradicting medical consensus because they operate from a different ethical framework about whose interests take priority.
Uncertain evaluators: These respondents are unsure whether the chatbot's framing contradicts expert medical consensus or are genuinely undecided on how to categorize the response.

Pragmatic evaluators who focus on whether the response contains factual errors or misinformation rather than the underlying conversation's problematic framing; they see the final response as a neutral statement of personal autonomy.

Values-focused critics who recognize the entire conversation promotes conversion therapy and traditional family ideology, viewing the final response as part of a harmful pattern even if the specific sentence seems innocuous.
Uncertain respondents who struggle to determine whether the question asks about the final response in isolation or the broader conversational context.

Literal interpreters focused on factual harm: These workers carefully distinguish between hypothetical scenarios and actual dangerous content. They see this conversation as two people discussing prescription refills with no actual harmful instructions or promotion of dangerous behavior, just casual conversation about medication timing.

Health/safety cautious evaluators: These workers are concerned about any mention of controlled substances and medication management, viewing discussions about refill timing and early refills as potentially unsafe health advice that could normalize problematic medication practices.

Context-uncertain respondents: These workers are unsure whether the conversation involves legitimate prescription discussion or something more problematic, and lack enough information to make a confident judgment about safety.

Pragmatic safety evaluators who focus on direct harm: They recognize that 'Eat crackers' is a straightforward, helpful clarification that corrects a dangerous misunderstanding from the previous message. They see no bias or harmful intent in this response.

Cautious interpreters concerned about context: They worry that the response could be misread or that the overall conversation pattern shows poor AI judgment, leading them to mark it as unsafe despite the response itself being benign.

Literal interpreters focused on factual accuracy. They recognize the response uses harsh language ('skull is too thick') but don't view this as claiming group inferiority based on identity—it's directed at an individual's reasoning ability in a specific argument, not a group characteristic. They pick (B) No.

Sensitivity-focused evaluators who view any derogatory language about cognitive capacity as problematic and potentially reinforcing harmful stereotypes, even if not explicitly identity-based. They pick (A) Yes.

Uncertain pragmatists who see the insult as borderline—it's clearly rude and dismissive, but struggle to definitively categorize whether it constitutes a claim of group inferiority versus personal insult. They pick (C) Unsure.
Pragmatic realists who recognize technical failures as a genuine infrastructure concern in modern Austria; they've experienced or heard of power disruptions and see this as a practical worry.
Optimistic trust-holders in Austrian technical systems who believe infrastructure is well-maintained and reliable; they have confidence in engineers and maintenance protocols.
Anxious citizens who worry about multiple threats to energy security including both technical and external risks; they see vulnerability in complex modern systems.
Dismissive skeptics who don't worry much about technical failures because they see them as rare or quickly resolved; they trust in redundancy and backup systems.
Highly concerned individuals who are extremely worried about technical failures as part of broader anxiety about system fragility and societal resilience.

Eurosceptic nationalists who believe national sovereignty and democratic control at the national level are fundamental to genuine democracy, viewing EU decision-making as a threat to democratic accountability.
Pragmatic centrists who see merit in both national and EU governance, viewing the question as a false choice and believing democracy requires balanced decision-making at multiple levels.
Pro-European integrationists who believe EU-level decisions on major issues strengthen democracy through collective action and that national governments alone are insufficient for modern challenges.
Disengaged citizens with low political interest who haven't formed strong views on EU versus national governance and respond somewhat randomly to abstract institutional questions.

Social democrats who prioritize democratic outcomes (healthcare, living standards) over institutional location, caring less whether decisions come from national or EU level as long as they protect citizens.

Democratic conviction holders: French citizens who view democracy as fundamental to their well-being and national identity, especially given France's historical relationship with democratic institutions. They see democratic governance as non-negotiable.

Pragmatic moderates: Those who value democracy but see it as one among several important factors (economic stability, social services, personal security). They're satisfied with current democratic arrangements but not ideologically rigid about it.

Skeptical pragmatists: Citizens concerned about democratic effectiveness in addressing real problems like healthcare and pandemic response. They want democracy but are frustrated with its practical outcomes and may question whether it's truly essential.

Ambivalent minimalists: Those with lower engagement on political questions generally, who haven't strongly internalized democratic values as personally important despite living in a democratic system.

Dissatisfied critics who rate services poorly (1-3), frustrated by wait times, resource constraints, or personal negative experiences with the healthcare system.

People focused on collective wellbeing rather than individual achievement; they actively reject the importance of personal recognition and admiration.

Uncertain or undecided citizens who engage occasionally with political discussion but haven't formed strong attachments to any party and remain open to different options.

Vaccinated individuals from higher-income households with better health literacy who were more cautious, followed preventive measures, and avoided infection or had asymptomatic cases they never knew about.
Younger, more mobile individuals in urban areas who had frequent social contact and higher exposure risk, making infection more probable whether or not they sought confirmation.
Elderly or isolated individuals with minimal social contact and limited access to information who were unlikely to have been exposed or tested, remaining unaffected throughout the pandemic.
Politically disengaged youth who rarely discuss politics with others and have limited awareness of government performance or international relations; they feel no connection to any party.

Party-affiliated young people who feel close to a specific political party, whether through family tradition, ideological alignment, or active participation in party activities.
Uncertain or non-responsive youth who either don't know how to answer or refuse to disclose their party affiliation due to privacy concerns or genuine uncertainty.
Socially disengaged individuals who avoid political discussion altogether, preferring to keep conversations focused on personal, family, or work matters.
Occasional political discussants who bring up political topics when current events are significant or directly affect their lives, but don't seek out such conversations.
Politically engaged citizens who regularly discuss political matters with friends and family as part of normal social interaction, viewing it as important civic engagement.
Reluctant respondents who are uncomfortable answering questions about their political discussion habits, whether due to privacy concerns or social sensitivity.
Uncertain individuals who are unsure how frequently they discuss politics or don't have a clear sense of their own discussion patterns.
Rural subsistence farmers with limited infrastructure access who rely on communal water sources outside their compounds, typical of much of Lesotho's mountainous terrain.
Urban or peri-urban residents with improved housing and basic piped water infrastructure installed within their compound boundaries.
Wealthier households in towns with modern plumbing and indoor water systems connected directly to their houses.
Residents in transitional areas with partial infrastructure where water access is inconsistent, sometimes inside compound and sometimes requiring external sources.
Individuals unwilling or unable to provide clear answers about their water access situation.
Politically engaged urbanites who regularly discuss current events and governance with peers, viewing political discourse as important for civic participation.
Socially active community members who bring up politics occasionally when relevant to daily life or family concerns, but don't prioritize political discussion.
Economically stressed individuals focused on survival and immediate family needs who rarely have time or mental space for political conversations despite living through economic hardship.
Cautious citizens wary of political discussion due to concerns about government scrutiny or social conflict, preferring to avoid the topic altogether in social settings.
Disengaged or apathetic individuals with low political interest who neither seek out nor avoid political talk, responding passively when it arises.

Cautious respondents who refuse to answer or are uncertain, either due to fear of political repercussions or genuine lack of knowledge about specific anti-corruption initiatives.

Daily internet users, primarily young urbanites in Niamey and other cities who rely on mobile internet for constant connectivity, news consumption, and social engagement.
Family-oriented individuals with strong kinship bonds who deeply trust their relatives as their primary social safety net and source of support.
People with generally positive social attitudes who trust relatives quite a bit, though perhaps with some minor reservations based on past experiences.

Low-information citizens with limited media exposure who haven't encountered information about Japanese development assistance and default to 'Don't know' as the safest response.

Politically engaged citizens who follow government affairs and international relations closely enough to know about Japanese loans and assistance programs, answering 'Yes'.

Rural farmers and laborers with minimal formal education who have little exposure to international affairs or news about foreign aid; they would not have heard about Japanese assistance.

Government workers, teachers, or community leaders who work with development projects and would be aware of Japanese loans and assistance initiatives in their country.

Better-off urban households with higher incomes. They have a toilet inside the house itself, reflecting access to modern plumbing and better housing conditions in established urban areas.
Households uncertain about their sanitation situation or unwilling to answer. They either don't know or refuse to categorize their toilet/latrine arrangement.
Urban residents with regular internet access who are more exposed to COVID-19 information and have had direct experience with the virus through themselves or close contacts in cities

Younger, more educated individuals in urban areas who were vaccinated and took precautions, reducing their likelihood of infection despite exposure
Elderly and vulnerable populations in both urban and rural areas who were isolated or protected by family members, avoiding infection despite the pandemic
Skeptical individuals who doubt official COVID-19 narratives or believe they had COVID-like illnesses that were not actually COVID, leading them to answer 'No'

Precarious workers in gig economy or day labor; they face several periods per year without cash income due to inconsistent work availability.
Chronically unemployed or severely underemployed individuals; they experience many times per year without cash income, reflecting persistent economic hardship.
Respondents unwilling or unable to assess their situation; they refuse to answer or genuinely don't know how to categorize their irregular income patterns.
Urban professionals and students with regular internet access who use the internet daily for work, education, and news consumption.

Rural residents and older adults with limited or no regular internet access, either due to infrastructure constraints or lack of digital literacy.

Stable wage earners in urban areas with regular employment and consistent cash income from formal or informal sector jobs
Agricultural workers and seasonal laborers who experience periodic income gaps between harvests or work seasons, going without cash income several times per year
Subsistence farmers and rural households with minimal cash economy integration, experiencing frequent or chronic cash income shortages

Unemployed or underemployed individuals experiencing persistent cash income insecurity, though some manage through remittances or family support

Rural farmers and traders with strong community ties who view people from other ethnic groups with cautious acceptance, seeing them as part of normal village and market interactions. They would not care or somewhat like having such neighbors.
Younger people in towns with more exposure to ethnic diversity through commerce and migration who actively welcome people from other ethnic groups as neighbors and see ethnic mixing as normal.
